explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Christ is the mediator of a new covenant so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. He has died to redeem them, and that's how it comes to them. An inheritance is something handed to you, not something you earn by working a double shift.

I get the guess, friend, because this chapter is crawling with priests. But the verse names something else: Christ is mediator so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. The verse says nothing about handing out priest jobs.

explanations.answer: A long life in the land
explanations.explanation: A long life sounds lovely, and I would take extra years in my bakery any day. But Hebrews 9:15 says those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance. Eternal, baker. That's a different size of gift than a few good decades.

Yes, baker. Christ died to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant (Hebrews 9:15). So His death reaches the transgressions from the first covenant. First is the word that fits.

Close, but this one's a mix-up. The new covenant is the one Christ mediates, and the verse says the transgressions were committed under the first covenant. His death redeems them from those sins. So the word you want is first.

Good eye, friend, because that word is in the verse. It just belongs to another spot: the promised eternal inheritance. The transgressions in question were committed under the first covenant (Hebrews 9:15). Right word, other oven.

explanations.answer: When the one who made it has died
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. A will does not take effect until the one who made it has died, and it cannot be executed while he is still alive (Hebrews 9:17). Nobody gets to cash in an inheritance while the person is still at the table eating cookies. The writer uses that everyday fact to explain why a death matters for the new covenant.

explanations.answer: When the whole family agrees to it
explanations.explanation: Everyone agreeing is a nice thought, friend. But Hebrews 9:17 says a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died. The writer never mentions anyone agreeing. It all hangs on that death.

explanations.answer: When it is read out in public
explanations.explanation: A big public reading sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But the writer says a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died (Hebrews 9:17). It can't be executed while he is still alive. Reading it out loud isn't what makes it work.

Yes, baker. Since a will needs a death, the first covenant was not put into effect without blood either (Hebrews 9:18). The writer ties the two together with a plain "That is why…" Moses shows what that looked like in the very next verses.

Incense is a good guess for a worship scene, friend. But the verse says the first covenant was not put into effect without blood (Hebrews 9:18). Incense isn't mentioned in these verses at all. The writer is following the will's death with the blood.

Silver would make a tidy price tag, but that's not what the writer says here. The first covenant was not put into effect without blood (Hebrews 9:18). The will needs a death, and the covenant needed blood.

explanations.answer: The scroll and all the people
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Moses sprinkled the scroll and all the people (Hebrews 9:19). The blood of calves and goats, with water, scarlet wool and hyssop, all went to that one moment. He even covered the people, so nobody was skipped.

Blood on doorposts does show up in Scripture, in Exodus 12:7. But that's not the scene Hebrews describes here. In this passage Moses sprinkles the scroll and all the people (Hebrews 9:19). Different blood, different moment.

explanations.answer: The fields and all the flocks
explanations.explanation: Fields and flocks are a fair guess, friend. But the text says Moses sprinkled the scroll and all the people (Hebrews 9:19). No mention of the fields, and no mention of a single sheep.
True, baker. Moses says, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.” (Hebrews 9:20) He speaks it as he sprinkles. The people hear exactly what the blood means.

This one is true, friend. Moses says, “This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep.” (Hebrews 9:20) He says it while sprinkling the people. I think it's easy to miss because the verse is short and it goes by fast.

explanations.answer: The tabernacle and its worship vessels
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. In the same way, Moses sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship (Hebrews 9:21). The scroll and the people were sprinkled first (Hebrews 9:19). Now the tabernacle and the vessels are covered too.

explanations.answer: The city gates and the walls
explanations.explanation: Gates and walls sound like a big job, but they're not in the verse. Hebrews 9:21 says he sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship. It's about the tabernacle and what was used in worship.

explanations.answer: The tents of the twelve tribes
explanations.explanation: That would take a long afternoon, friend, and the writer doesn't say it. Hebrews 9:21 says Moses sprinkled the tabernacle and all the vessels used in worship. The tribes' own tents never come up.

You got it, baker. “…without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” (Hebrews 9:22) The writer says nearly everything is purified with blood under the law. Forgiveness is the heart of that line, so hold onto it.
Rest is a lovely word, and I could use some after a long bake. But the verse says, “…without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” (Hebrews 9:22) That's what the writer is driving at.

Wisdom is a good thing to want, friend, but that's not the word here. The writer says, “…without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.” (Hebrews 9:22) Forgiveness is what the blood is about in this verse.

Yes, baker. The copies of the heavenly things were purified with these sacrifices, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these (Hebrews 9:23). The copies get one kind and the real thing gets better ones. Think of it like practice dough and the batch that goes in the box.

Smaller is a fair guess, friend, but the verse goes another way. It says the heavenly things themselves needed better sacrifices than these (Hebrews 9:23). It's about quality, and the text doesn't say a word about size.

Older doesn't fit, baker. The verse says it was necessary for the heavenly things themselves to be purified with better sacrifices than these (Hebrews 9:23). The writer is comparing the copies with the real thing, and he calls the sacrifices better.

That's right, baker. Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself (Hebrews 9:24). He went to the real place, not a copy built by hands. And He is there now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.

Mount Sinai is a place people remember, friend, but it isn't in this verse. Hebrews 9:24 says He did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself. He went to the true place, not to a spot on earth.
Eden is a fine place to picture, but it's not what the writer says. Christ entered heaven itself (Hebrews 9:24). The writer sets that against a man-made copy of the true sanctuary.

True, baker. He entered heaven itself, “…now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.” (Hebrews 9:24) That's "…on our behalf…" so it's for us. A friend standing in the right room for you is no small thing.

This one is true, friend. The verse says He entered heaven itself, “…now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God.” (Hebrews 9:24) He's there for us, in the presence of God. It's a good one to remember.

This one is false, baker, and the writer says so plainly. Nor did He enter heaven to offer Himself again and again, as the high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own (Hebrews 9:25). The high priest comes back every year, but Christ does not. His offering is not repeated.

Right, baker. Hebrews 9:25 says Christ did not enter heaven to offer Himself again and again. The high priest enters the Most Holy Place every year with blood that is not his own. Christ's offering is not a yearly one like that.

explanations.answer: He would have suffered over and over since the world began
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Otherwise, the writer says, Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world (Hebrews 9:26). That's a lot of suffering, and the writer says it didn't go that way. Instead He appeared once for all.

explanations.answer: Moses would have sprinkled the people every single year
explanations.explanation: Moses is in this passage, friend, but not in this verse. The writer says Christ would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world (Hebrews 9:26). The point is about Christ's offering, not a yearly sprinkling.

explanations.answer: The tabernacle would have had to be rebuilt in heaven
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but the writer never says that. Christ entered heaven itself (Hebrews 9:24), and the verse says that otherwise He would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world (Hebrews 9:26). Nothing there about rebuilding anything.
Yes, baker. Christ “…was offered once to bear the sins of many…” (Hebrews 9:28). Man dies once, and Christ was offered once. The writer lines those two up side by side.
Prayers are a good thing, friend, but that's not the word here. The verse says Christ “…was offered once to bear the sins of many…” (Hebrews 9:28). Sins is the word the writer uses.
Praises are wonderful, baker, and I give plenty of them. But Hebrews 9:28 says Christ “…was offered once to bear the sins of many…” That's what He bore.

This one is false, baker. The writer says Christ “…will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.” (Hebrews 9:28) The bearing of sin was done once. Next time He comes with salvation.

Yes, baker. Hebrews 9:28 says He “…will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.” The bearing of sin was already done once (Hebrews 9:26, 28). The second appearing is for salvation.

That's right, baker. He will bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him (Hebrews 9:28). Eagerly is the word. Nobody knows the day or hour (Matthew 24:36), so I keep my oven mitts handy and I keep waiting.

explanations.answer: The priests who served the tabernacle
explanations.explanation: The priests are all over this chapter, friend, so I see why you went there. But the verse says He will bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him (Hebrews 9:28). It doesn't name the priests at all.

explanations.answer: Everyone who kept the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Moses and the law get a lot of space in this passage, baker. But the verse says He will bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him (Hebrews 9:28). Those who kept the law aren't named there.
